chapter_title: The Abstract Factory Pattern: Families of Related Objects

screens.title: Abstract Factory Pattern
screens.subtitle: Creating families of related objects without fixing concrete classes

narration.text: In this lesson we'll explore the Abstract Factory pattern and why it matters when you need coherent sets of objects. The pattern provides an interface to create related or dependent products so client code works with abstract types only. A concrete factory produces a matching family of products, for example Windows UI elements or Mac UI elements, so a button and a checkbox belong to the same family and remain compatible. You will see how the pattern separates what varies from what stays the same, enabling platform independence and consistent behavior across a system. We will use a GUI toolkit example to show interfaces for buttons and checkboxes, concrete products for each platform, and factory implementations that bundle them together. You'll also work through a database connector lab that applies the same idea to connection and command objects. By the end you should be able to decide when Abstract Factory is the right tool, how to implement it in C#, and what trade-offs to weigh when teams must add new product types or families. Consider where you currently mix incompatible objects in your code—could a factory family enforce compatibility?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Provide interfaces to create related objects so entire product families can be swapped without changing client code.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Overview
Abstract Factory Pattern
Create families of related objects without specifying concrete classes.

When a system needs sets of compatible objects, the Abstract Factory lets you obtain a full suite of implementations that work together. This reduces the risk of mixing incompatible concrete types and centralizes platform-specific code.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will do four concrete things. First, identify the problem the Abstract Factory solves: producing families of related objects without tying code to concrete classes. Second, distinguish and name the pattern roles: abstract product, concrete product, abstract factory, concrete factory, and client. Third, implement a simple Abstract Factory in C# so your client code can request a family of objects from a single factory interface. Fourth, evaluate when to use Abstract Factory by weighing benefits like consistency and platform independence against costs such as more interfaces and required changes when adding new product types. For example, you will implement a GUI factory that returns matching button and checkbox instances for Windows and Mac, and you will also apply the same idea to database connection and command families. These skills let you design systems that enforce compatibility across components and keep client code open to new families without direct modification. Keep these objectives in mind as you work through the examples and lab.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (continued)
screens.subtitle: Skills and decisions you will master

narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on judgment and extension. You will learn to identify appropriate use cases for Abstract Factory in complex systems, such as ensuring UI components or database objects remain compatible. You will practice the difference between adding a new product family versus adding a new product type. Adding a new family is easy: introduce a new concrete factory and concrete products. Adding a new product type, however, requires modifying the abstract factory interface and all concrete factories, which can be costly. We'll also cover common misconceptions: Abstract Factory is not a replacement for Factory Method when you only need to create one product type. Finally, you will complete a short hands-on activity to reinforce implementation details and to practice designing the factory interfaces so they remain extensible yet maintainable. These decisions are central to good design, because they balance consistency against flexibility in your codebase.

keyIdea.title: Decision guidance
keyIdea.text: Use Abstract Factory when you need fully compatible product families; avoid it when you only need one variable product type.

screens.title: What Abstract Factory Solves
screens.subtitle: Creating families of related or dependent objects

narration.text: The Abstract Factory pattern addresses a very specific design problem: you need sets of objects that are designed to work together and you must avoid mixing implementations from different families. Define abstract product interfaces for each product type you need, and define an abstract factory interface that groups creation methods for those products. Concrete factories implement that interface to produce concrete products belonging to one coherent family. A practical example is a cross-platform UI: if you mix a Windows button with a Mac checkbox you break visual consistency and possibly behavior. The Abstract Factory solves this by ensuring the client requests products only through abstract interfaces and receives a consistent set from a single factory. A common misconception is that this pattern always reduces code; it does not. It increases the number of interfaces and classes but provides a strong guarantee of compatibility and makes switching platforms trivial. For a concrete example, imagine toggling a single factory instance at startup to switch the whole UI theme. What effect would this have on your application's testing and maintenance? What Abstract Factory Solves means ensures a client obtains compatible products by centralizing family creation through an abstract factory interface.. In practical terms, creating families of related or dependent objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Problem solved
keyIdea.text: Ensures a client obtains compatible products by centralizing family creation through an abstract factory interface.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › What Abstract Factory Solves
Definition
An interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying concrete classes.
• Define an abstract product interface for each product type you need.
• Create an abstract factory that declares creation methods for all abstract products.
• Implement concrete factories that return concrete products of a single family.
Key Takeaway

Abstract Factory enforces product compatibility by providing a single entry point for creating related products.

Concrete example
Cross-platform UI: IButton and ICheckbox are abstract products. WindowsGUIFactory returns WindowsButton and WindowsCheckbox so both controls match visually and semantically.
Common misconception
People sometimes use Abstract Factory when only one product needs variation. In that case Factory Method is simpler.
Why it matters
Consistency across product sets reduces integration bugs.

screens.title: Participants: Roles and Relationships
screens.subtitle: Abstract Product, Concrete Product, Abstract Factory, Concrete Factory, Client

narration.text: The Abstract Factory pattern is organized around five key participants. First, Abstract Product: an interface or abstract class representing a product type such as a button or checkbox. Second, Concrete Product: a family-specific implementation of an abstract product, for example WindowsButton or MacCheckbox. Third, Abstract Factory: an interface declaring methods to create each abstract product. Fourth, Concrete Factory: a class that implements the abstract factory and returns concrete products belonging to the same family. Finally, the Client uses only the abstract factory and abstract products. The client never depends on concrete classes, which lets you swap factories at runtime or during configuration. A useful mental model is a hierarchy where the abstract factory is the parent of factory implementations, and abstract products are parents to concrete products across families. One common pitfall is coupling the client to a concrete factory directly; that defeats the purpose. Always program to interfaces and inject the factory so tests and platform swaps become simple and safe. Participants: Roles and Relationships means abstract and concrete products plus an abstract factory and concrete factories; the client depends only on the abstract interfaces.. In practical terms, abstract product, concrete product, abstract factory, concrete factory, client. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Participants
keyIdea.text: Abstract and concrete products plus an abstract factory and concrete factories; the client depends only on the abstract interfaces.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Participants
Role hierarchy
Think of roles as two hierarchies: one for products and one for factories. The abstract factory groups product creation methods that return abstract products from the product hierarchy.
• Abstract Product: contract that all concrete products for a given type must satisfy.
• Concrete Product: a platform-specific implementation of that contract.
• Abstract Factory: declares factory methods for each abstract product.
• Concrete Factory: implements the methods to produce a consistent family.
• Client: composes with the abstract factory and abstract products only.

Product Hierarchy
IButton → WindowsButton
Pitfall
If the client instantiates concrete factories directly, you lose interchangeability and testability.

screens.title: Abstract Products and Concrete Products (C#)
screens.subtitle: Interfaces for IButton and ICheckbox with Windows and Mac implementations

narration.text: Let's inspect the C# interfaces and concrete product implementations for our GUI example. The Abstract Products are interfaces like IButton and ICheckbox. Concrete products implement those interfaces per platform. For example, WindowsButton implements IButton and returns a Windows-specific rendering string. WindowsCheckbox implements ICheckbox and maintains its own internal checked state. The Mac family provides MacButton and MacCheckbox with their platform-specific behavior. Reading these implementations clarifies why the client can treat them uniformly: both families satisfy the same contracts. A common mistake is embedding platform-specific logic into the client instead of the concrete products; keep platform behavior inside concrete classes. Now look at the code example shown. Note how each concrete class implements the same interface methods, so swapping families requires no client changes. Think about testing: you can supply test doubles that implement IButton and ICheckbox to verify client logic without creating real UI elements. How would this affect your integration tests? Abstract Products and Concrete Products (C#) means abstract products define a stable contract; concrete products implement platform-specific behavior behind that contract.. In practical terms, interfaces for ibutton and icheckbox with windows and mac implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Product contracts
keyIdea.text: Abstract products define a stable contract; concrete products implement platform-specific behavior behind that contract.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Products: GUI
Abstract and Concrete Products
Below is the C# code for product interfaces and two concrete families. Read it to see how contracts are shared.
// Abstract Products: Interfaces for a family of related products.
public interface IButton
{
    string Render();
}

public interface ICheckbox
{
    string Render();
    bool IsChecked();
}

// Concrete Products: Implementations for Windows family
public class WindowsButton : IButton
{
    public string Render() => "Rendering a Windows-style button.";
}

public class WindowsCheckbox : ICheckbox
{
    private bool _checked = false;
    public string Render() => $"Rendering a Windows-style checkbox (Checked: {_checked}).";
    public bool IsChecked() => _checked;
}

// Concrete Products: Implementations for Mac family
public class MacButton : IButton
{
    public string Render() => "Rendering a Mac-style button.";
}

public class MacCheckbox : ICheckbox
{
    private bool _checked = true;
    public string Render() => $"Rendering a Mac-style checkbox (Checked: {_checked}).";
    public bool IsChecked() => _checked;
}
Explanation
  • Both families implement identical methods so clients can call Render and IsChecked without platform logic.
  • Concrete products encapsulate platform-specific state and representation.
  • Tests can mock these interfaces to validate client behavior independently of UI frameworks.
Example
Switching factories changes visuals globally without client changes.

narration.text: Now we examine the factory interfaces and concrete factories that produce matching product families. The abstract factory declares creation methods such as CreateButton and CreateCheckbox. Concrete factories like WindowsGUIFactory and MacGUIFactory implement these methods to return platform-specific concrete products. The critical design point is that the client receives an IGUIFactory reference. It calls factory methods and uses only abstract product interfaces. This lets you substitute a Windows factory for a Mac factory with no client changes. A misconception is assuming factories must be static; in practice factories are often injected or created at application start so swapping is straightforward. Consider dependency injection here: register the desired concrete factory and resolve it in client constructors. The code below shows how these interfaces and classes are defined in C#. Notice how simple the factory methods are: they just instantiate concrete products, but that indirection gives you a powerful way to manage entire product families. Abstract Factory and Concrete Factories (C#) means the abstract factory groups creation methods; concrete factories return family-specific product instances.. In practical terms, iguifactory, windowsguifactory, macguifactory implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Factory contract
keyIdea.text: The abstract factory groups creation methods; concrete factories return family-specific product instances.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Factory implementations
Factory interfaces and classes
The abstract factory groups creation methods so clients can request a suite of products from a single object.
// Abstract Factory: Declares an interface for operations that create abstract product objects.
public interface IGUIFactory
{
    IButton CreateButton();
    ICheckbox CreateCheckbox();
}

// Concrete Factories: Implement the factory methods to create concrete product objects.
public class WindowsGUIFactory : IGUIFactory
{
    public IButton CreateButton() => new WindowsButton();
    public ICheckbox CreateCheckbox() => new WindowsCheckbox();
}

public class MacGUIFactory : IGUIFactory
{
    public IButton CreateButton() => new MacButton();
    public ICheckbox CreateCheckbox() => new MacCheckbox();
}
Notes
  • Concrete factories create all products in one family, ensuring compatibility.
  • Factories are usually injected so configuration drives which family is active.
  • Adding a new factory for another platform requires implementing the factory and concrete products only.
Pro tip
Keep factory methods coarse-grained to reduce interface churn when adding types.

screens.title: Client Code and Runtime Behavior
screens.subtitle: Application creates product family through a factory

narration.text: This screen examines the client code that consumes the abstract factory and products. The Application class accepts an IGUIFactory in its constructor, then asks the factory to create a button and a checkbox. When Paint runs, it calls the Render method on each product and uses IsChecked for the checkbox. The Program class shows a simple runtime switch: instantiate Application with a Windows factory, then with a Mac factory. The client is oblivious to concrete types—it calls methods defined on abstract products. This separation supports platform independence and simplifies swapping implementations for testing or deployment. A common mistake is to perform type checks or casts in the client; avoid that. If you need platform-specific behavior, implement it inside concrete products or provide extension hooks on the factory. Reading the sample run demonstrates how different output appears for different factories while client code remains identical. How could this pattern simplify feature toggles that change UI families at runtime? Client Code and Runtime Behavior means clients depend only on abstract factories and products, enabling runtime family swaps without client changes.. In practical terms, application creates product family through a factory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Client independence
keyIdea.text: Clients depend only on abstract factories and products, enabling runtime family swaps without client changes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Client: Application
Client code
The client composes with the abstract factory and uses only abstract product members.
// Client: Uses the Abstract Factory and Abstract Products.
public class Application
{
    private IGUIFactory _factory;
    private IButton _button;
    private ICheckbox _checkbox;

    public Application(IGUIFactory factory)
    {
        _factory = factory;
        _button = _factory.CreateButton();
        _checkbox = _factory.CreateCheckbox();
    }

    public void Paint()
    {
        Console.WriteLine(_button.Render());
        Console.WriteLine(_checkbox.Render());
        Console.WriteLine($"Is checkbox checked? {_checkbox.IsChecked()}");
    }
}

public class Program
{
    public static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("--- Windows Application ---");
        Application windowsApp = new Application(new WindowsGUIFactory());
        windowsApp.Paint();
        Console.WriteLine();

        Console.WriteLine("--- Mac Application ---");
        Application macApp = new Application(new MacGUIFactory());
        macApp.Paint();
        Console.WriteLine();
    }
}
Runtime behavior
  • Swap the concrete factory to change the entire family returned to the client.
  • Client code remains unchanged; only factory instantiation differs.
  • Dependency injection makes switching and testing straightforward.
Example output
Windows and Mac runs show different Render strings but identical client calls.

screens.title: Benefits vs. Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: When Abstract Factory helps and when it costs too much

narration.text: Abstract Factory brings clear benefits and some costs. Benefits include product compatibility, platform independence, and alignment with the Open/Closed Principle because adding new product families does not change client code. It centralizes platform-specific creation and reduces runtime mixing of incompatible components. However, the pattern also introduces complexity: more interfaces and classes, and a larger surface area to update if you add a new product type. Adding a new type requires modifying the abstract factory interface and every concrete factory. This is the primary trade-off: easy to add families, costly to add product types. Use Abstract Factory when compatibility matters, such as UI toolkits or connectors where objects must work together. For simpler needs, Factory Method or a simple factory is often preferable. Consider development velocity and frequency of product-type additions when choosing the pattern. Ask yourself: will I be adding new platforms more often than new product types? Benefits vs. Trade-offs means great for family consistency and platform swaps; costly if product types change often because interfaces must be updated.. In practical terms, when abstract factory helps and when it costs too much. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Benefits
  • Ensures consistency among related products.
  • Makes switching product families straightforward.
  • Supports platform-independent client code and easier testing.
Design win
Ideal when families need to be kept coherent.
Trade-offs

screens.title: Abstract Factory vs Factory Method
screens.subtitle: When to prefer one pattern over the other

narration.text: People often conflate Abstract Factory with Factory Method, so let's contrast them clearly. Factory Method focuses on creating a single product and uses inheritance so subclasses decide which concrete product to instantiate. It's a good fit when you need to vary one product type and let subclasses override creation without changing the client. Abstract Factory, by contrast, groups several factory methods inside a single interface to create families of related products. It uses composition: a factory object contains the methods for creating multiple products. If your problem requires maintaining compatibility among several product types, Abstract Factory is the better choice. If only one product needs to vary, Factory Method usually keeps code simpler. Another misconception is that Abstract Factory always replaces Factory Method; in fact, both can be used together: an abstract factory might internally use factory methods to build some products. Think about how many product axes your system has before picking a pattern. Abstract Factory vs Factory Method means factory method varies a single product via inheritance; abstract factory produces multiple related products via composition.. In practical terms, when to prefer one pattern over the other. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern contrast
keyIdea.text: Factory Method varies a single product via inheritance; Abstract Factory produces multiple related products via composition.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Abstract Factory vs Factory Method
Factory Method
Creates one product. Uses subclassing so subclasses decide which concrete product to create. Simpler for single product variation.
When to use
One product varies by subclass behavior.
Abstract Factory
Creates many related products. Uses a factory object that exposes creation methods for each product. Best when you need compatible product families.
When to use
Multiple product types must be consistent within families.

screens.title: Lab: Database Connector Factory
screens.subtitle: Starter code walkthrough and TODOs for SQL Server and Oracle families

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to implement an Abstract Factory that returns compatible database connection and command objects per database family. The starter code defines abstract products IDbConnection and IDbCommand, plus concrete SqlServerConnection and SqlServerCommand. Your task is to implement OracleConnection, OracleCommand, and OracleFactory so the DatabaseClient can use either factory interchangeably. Key details: IDbCommand must accept an IDbConnection via SetConnection so it can execute against the right connection. The DatabaseClient asks the factory for a connection and a command, wires them together, opens the connection, executes a query, then closes the connection. A common error is creating a command that assumes a specific connection type; instead, commands should rely on the abstract IDbConnection contract. After completing the starter TODOs, instantiate the OracleFactory in Main and verify the console output shows Oracle-specific messages. As an extension, consider adding an IDbTransaction product and observe that you must modify IDbFactory and all concrete factories for full support. public class DatabaseClient
{
    private IDbFactory _factory;
    private IDbConnection _connection;
    private IDbCommand _command;
